coverage.assessment: The Pendennis joke, the Newton analogy and the Agassiz insertion survive. Two causal links are cut: why Adams resorted to the inserted sentence, and the publish-or-not dilemma that gives 'labor and caution' its point.
Wenlock and the Milnes Gaskells are glossed and Ara Coeli is dated to 1860. The close drops the London-season transition, so Rome jumps to London and then to Liverpool.
There is no performed dialogue. The quoted Agassiz sentence and the La Fontaine verse are preserved intact and correctly framed.

The revision makes the boy, not Murchison, the namer of the Limulus. The 'five thousand millions' price matches the earlier 'five or ten thousand million' statement. Walcott and Colorado are correctly absent.
The 'sacrificed much more' retrospect survives. The loss of the 'thirty years to wait' retrospect is treated under F8.
The anchors are intact. The lyrical Wenlock passage and several comic beats (Lyell's ready assent, the audacity of youth) are reduced to bare statement.
The confession loses its contrast with other Darwinians' faith, the father's reaction, and the Oxford-degree irony. This weakens the turn toward Unity as Will.
All three dependencies survive at both endpoints in the abridged texts of 028 and 022.

dependencies.assessment: The local text names Pteraspis as ganoid ancestor and nearest relative seen from Wenlock Edge, and 'Ludlow shale' survives. The Twilight callback 'oldest friend and cousin ... Pteraspis of Ludlow and Wenlock' is kept in 028.

dependencies.assessment: The Quincy Bay horseshoe memory, the Limulus line and Terebratula's identity across geological time survive locally, apart from the naming slip in F5. The Braintree Limulus callback is kept in 028.

certain forms, like Terebratula, appeared to be identical from the beginning to the end of geological time

dependencies.assessment: The revision shows Adams writing the Lyell piece and then credits 'the review of Lyell' with his place on the Review's staff. 022 keeps 'Thanks to the article on Sir Charles Lyell'.

Thanks to the article on Sir Charles Lyell, Adams passed for a friend of geologists.

findings.claim: The revision drops the constraint that Adams could not tell Lyell his doubts yet was obliged to state Lyell's views, which he thought worthless. 'Adams hinted his heresies in vain' now follows the rhetorical question directly.
findings.counterevidence: The phrase 'bold experiment ... intended to provoke correction' still implies he lacked a direct channel.

evidence.quote: Naturally a young man, altogether ignorant, could not say this to Sir Charles Lyell or Sir Isaac Newton; but he was forced to state Sir Charles's views
Naturally a young man, altogether ignorant, could not say this to Sir Charles Lyell; but he was forced to state Sir Charles's views, which he thought weak as hypotheses and worthless as proofs.
If the glacial period were uniformity, what was catastrophe? Adams hinted his heresies in vain.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's sentence 'Naturally a young man ... worthless as proofs.' before 'Adams hinted'.
findings.plan_relation: required (glacial doubt and the inserted sentence are essential)
findings.reader_effect: The 'bold experiment' of smuggling a sentence into the text loses its comic logic: a junior forced to transmit theories he could not openly dispute.
findings.title: Motive for the inserted Agassiz sentence cut

findings.claim: The revision cuts several elements the first draft kept: Shropshire as 'the part of his diplomatic education which he loved best', the list of Wrekin, Ludlow and Abbey pleasures, the Welsh-thief image and the 'mix up the terms of time' sentence. 'Liked best' and 'the triumph of all' now lack the series they top. 'An American in search of a father' is also cut.
findings.counterevidence: The core anchors survive ('One's instinct abhors time', the Roman road and railroad pairing, Pteraspis and the Cambrian void). The place-name list was optional.

evidence.quote: By this time, in 1867 Adams had learned to know Shropshire familiarly, and it was the part of his diplomatic education which he loved best.
To an American in search of a father, it mattered nothing whether the father breathed through lungs, or walked on fins, or on feet.
The shepherds of Caractacus or Offa, or the monks of Buildwas, had they approached where he lay in the grass, would have taken him only for another and tamer variety of Welsh thief.
Adams liked best to ramble over the Edge on a summer afternoon and look across the Marches to the mountains of Wales.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's opening sentence on Shropshire, the Welsh-thief sentence, and the 'American in search of a father' sentence.
findings.plan_relation: required (the risks section asks that this voice not be flattened); the first draft's level of cutting was adequate
findings.reader_effect: The plan's heaviest section loses the evidence that time-sequences are interchangeable and much of its lyrical rhythm. It also loses the attachment that explains why the last English year was the happiest.
findings.title: Wenlock meditation flattened; comparatives left dangling

findings.claim: The revision drops three elements. The other Darwinians' dogmatic faith ('Adams wished no better') no longer frames his lack of Faith. The father's annoyance and the son's greater annoyance, with the Hamlet aside, are gone, so 'To him, the current of his time' follows 'sacrilege!' with no turn. The 'Oxford degree' close is removed.
findings.counterevidence: Paragraph 13 still has 'he determined to stop it', which partly motivates the resolve.

evidence.quote: To other Darwinians--except Darwin--Natural Selection seemed a dogma to be put in the place of the Athanasian creed; it was a form of religious hope
but it did not annoy him nearly so much as it annoyed his son, who had no need to learn from Hamlet the fatal effect of the pale cast of thought
Mr. Adams, the father, looked on it as moral weakness; it annoyed him; but it did not annoy him nearly so much as it annoyed his son
From the beginning of history, this attitude had been branded as criminal--worse than crime--sacrilege! To him, the current of his time was to be his current, lead where it might.
This was the result of five or six years in England; a result so British as to be almost the equivalent of an Oxford degree.

findings.plan_relation: required (keep one of Bluebeard/Hamlet); the confession and resolve are essential
findings.reader_effect: The resolve to lock up psychology reads as a non sequitur rather than self-coercion against his own skepticism. The plan explicitly asked to keep one of the Bluebeard or Hamlet asides.

findings.counterevidence: 'Or' can be read as the narrator's gloss, so the error is ambiguous rather than flatly false.

In Siluria, he understood, Sir Roderick Murchison called the horseshoe a Limulus, which helped nothing.
in search of the fascinating creature he had called a horseshoe, or Limulus, whose huge dome of shell and sharp spur of tail had so alarmed him as a child.

findings.claim: Adams no longer 'found nothing simpler than to suggest'. 'Youth risks such encounters with the universe' is gone, as is his surprise at Lyell's ready assent after half an hour. All of this becomes 'Sir Charles assented'.
findings.counterevidence: 'This was getting on fast; Arthur Pendennis had never gone so far' is intact.

findings.claim: The revision drops two framing passages. One is Adams's self-question over the editor's letter that frames the list of contemporaries. The other is the shift in Anglo-American strength, with its 1868-to-1898 retrospect ('thirty years to wait').
findings.counterevidence: 'Silurian horizon', 'summer sea' and 'could have chosen no better path' survive.

strengths: All eight verbatim anchors survive in context, including the paradox sentence and 'He was a Darwinian for fun.'
The Pocahontas reference is cleanly glossed as 'his earlier historical article', and the Milnes Gaskells are identified at the Abbey.
The 'five or ten thousand million' and 'five thousand millions more' prices are both kept and agree, along with the 'sacrificed much more' retrospect.
'Silurian horizon' at the close still echoes the Pteraspis kingdom, and the worn-suit image ends the chapter intact.
summary: The revision keeps the chapter's argument, all eight verbatim anchors, the Pteraspis, Limulus and Terebratula emblems, and the local glosses for the Milnes Gaskells and the earlier article. It has no blocking errors. It cuts much harder than the first draft, though, and several cuts made only in this pass thin the execution. The Wenlock meditation loses its comparative and series structure. The turn from 'Darwinian for fun' to locking up psychology loses its father/Hamlet motive. The specie-payments publishing dilemma disappears. The Limulus name is misattributed. The Rome-to-London close jumps without a transition. These are editorial repairs, not structural failures.
